metrics.label: Forward P/E
metrics.description: Price relative to expected next-year earnings; sourced from ticker.info forwardPE.
metrics.calculation: Share price ÷ forecast earnings per share for next year (Yahoo forwardPE).
metrics.interpretation: Higher = the market pays more per dollar of expected profit (priced for quality/growth, or simply expensive). Always read next to growth.
metrics.applicability: Undefined for loss-makers (negative or near-zero forecast earnings) — the value is meaningless, not "cheap."
metrics.analogy: Think payback time: how many years of expected earnings are priced into one share today.
metrics.learn: P/E (price-to-earnings) divides the share price by earnings per share. Forward P/E uses analyst estimates for next year's earnings, not last year's results. A higher number often means investors expect faster growth — or are paying a premium today.

metrics.label: Operating margin (TTM)
metrics.description: TTM operating income divided by TTM total revenue (four quarterly statements), times 100; falls back to latest annual when four quarters are unavailable, with the basis recorded in ebit_margin_basis. Not Yahoo's single-quarter operatingMargins.
metrics.calculation: Operating profit ÷ revenue × 100 (trailing twelve months from four quarters; latest annual as fallback).
metrics.interpretation: Higher = more of each sales dollar kept as operating profit. Stable high margins signal pricing power and efficiency.
metrics.applicability: Breaks for pre-revenue firms (revenue ≈ 0 → explodes); means something different for financials.
metrics.gloss: Operating profit as share of sales (TTM)
metrics.analogy: For every dollar of sales, this is the slice kept as operating profit before interest and taxes.
metrics.learn: This card sums Operating Income and Total Revenue from the last four quarterly financial statements, then divides — a trailing twelve-month (TTM) operating margin. It is not Yahoo's single-quarter operatingMargins snapshot.

metrics.label: Rev growth YoY (quarter)
metrics.description: Latest reported quarter revenue versus the same quarter a year ago (ticker.info revenueGrowth, times 100).
metrics.calculation: Latest quarter revenue vs the same quarter a year ago (Yahoo revenueGrowth × 100).
metrics.interpretation: Higher = faster top-line growth — but growth ≠ health (a company can grow into losses). Single quarter, so noisy.
metrics.applicability: Distorted by tiny prior-year bases (micro-caps, commodity ramps → huge % off a small base).
metrics.gloss: Sales growth vs same quarter last year
metrics.analogy: Compared with a year ago — is the business growing, flat, or shrinking?
metrics.learn: Year-over-year (YoY) growth compares revenue in the latest reported quarter with the same quarter one year ago (Yahoo revenueGrowth). One quarter can be noisy — look for a pattern over time when you dig deeper.

metrics.label: Net debt / EBITDA
metrics.description: Net debt (info_net_debt, or info_total_debt minus info_total_cash) divided by Yahoo EBITDA; periods may differ. A rough leverage signal, not a precise accounting ratio.
metrics.calculation: (Total debt − cash) ÷ EBITDA — roughly how many years of earnings to clear net debt.
metrics.interpretation: Lower = less leverage, safer. Negative = net cash. High = exposed in downturns or when rates rise.
metrics.applicability: Meaningless for financials ("cash" includes customer/policyholder assets); explodes when EBITDA ≈ 0 (distressed/pre-profit).
metrics.analogy: If operating profit stayed steady, about how many years to repay net debt from cash generation?
metrics.learn: Net debt is total debt minus cash on hand (Yahoo). EBITDA is Yahoo's reported EBITDA figure — often trailing, not necessarily matched to the same instant as the balance sheet. Use this as a rough leverage signal, not a precise accounting ratio.

metrics.label: FCF margin (annual)
metrics.description: Free cash flow divided by total revenue (latest annual cash flow and income statements), times 100.
metrics.calculation: Free cash flow ÷ revenue × 100 (latest annual statements).
metrics.interpretation: Higher = more real cash per sales dollar — harder to fake than accounting profit. The strongest single health signal.
metrics.applicability: Breaks for pre-revenue firms (revenue ≈ 0); not meaningful for financials.
metrics.gloss: Free cash left from each sales dollar (latest annual statements)
metrics.analogy: After running the business, how much cash is left from each sales dollar — not the same as accounting profit.
metrics.learn: Free cash flow (FCF) is cash left after running and investing in the business. This card computes FCF margin from the latest annual cash flow and income statements — not Yahoo's trailing Key Statistics ratio. Run the metric audit script to compare.
